meta.title: Polish A2
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Polish → English (see the Polish, recall the meaning) and English → Polish (see an English meaning, recall the Polish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words for level A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Poland's State Commission for the Certification of Proficiency in Polish as a Foreign Language examines at all six levels, but no official word list was found for any of them. So 648 of the 750 words were written for Folio, a topic at a time, for the topics the A2 exam is described as covering — thanking, apologising, inviting, good wishes and congratulations, feelings and opinions, place, direction and time, quantity and quality, describing and comparing people, table manners, Polish dishes and mealtimes, name days, birthdays and visits, clothes for official occasions, renting a flat, the telephone, the doctor, school and work, travel in Poland and Europe, and cultural and artistic life — together with the modal words (trzeba, warto, należy), the verbs of motion, the feminine names for people (studentka beside student) and the conjunctions the level's grammar names. They are Folio's choice, not the Commission's, and this is not an official word list. No word taught in the levels below is repeated. The other 102 are the commonest words of everyday Polish not already chosen, from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles, each word counted over all its forms. The cards are ordered by that frequency, so the words met most often come first; the 14 set phrases, which a list of single words cannot count, come last. Polish changes the endings of its nouns, adjectives and verbs, and many stems change with them, so each card carries the forms that cannot be guessed, read from a dictionary rather than generated. 393 nouns show their gender, three cases of the singular and two of the plural. 165 verbs show their aspect and its partner, the forms for ja (I), on (he) and oni (they) and the past of on — a perfective verb's being its future, since it has no present. 70 adjectives show their comparative and superlative. One pronoun shows its cases. Real example sentences come with 718 of the 750 words, three apiece for 651, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Meanings, forms and parts of speech: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency ordering: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
